overview: White fianchettoes the queen's bishop with Bb2 to hit e5 and the long diagonal, and Black usually responds with a kingside fianchetto of their own after 2...g6. Both sides aim at the centre from the flanks and the position is usually quiet and flexible. White chooses e3, Nf3 and a later c4 or f4 depending on Black's set-up.

white_ideas.idea: Bb2 on the long diagonal, then e3, Nf3 and a late c4 or f4
Trade the dark-squared bishops or exploit the long diagonal against e5/g7
Delay central pawn commitment and react to Black's set-up

black_ideas.idea: Mirror with ...g6 and Bg7, fianchetto and meet Bb2 with the same diagonal
Build the centre with ...d6 and ...e5 or ...c5
Develop smoothly, castle and wait for White's central commitment

typical_structures.structure: Double fianchetto with flexible, undecided centre
White e3/d3 against Black ...d6/...e5 with both long diagonals contested

character.notes: Quiet manoeuvring, few forced sequences. Both sides can switch plans.

structure.notes: Flank opening with the centre undecided; flexible like the English.

approach.notes: Bb2/e3/Nf3 set-up used against many defences, close to a system, though 1.b3 is a recognised offbeat-ish alternative.

level.notes: Little theory but needs feel for when to strike with c4 or f4, intermediate.

sublines_that_differ.name: Nimzo-Larsen: 2.Bb2 e6 Classical
sublines_that_differ.how: Black keeps the centre flexible and may go for a Queen's Indian structure.

character.reason: Quiet flank play, neither especially solid nor sharp.

approach.reason: Bb2, e3, Nf3 set-up playable against almost any reply.

level.reason: Plans are subtle but there is little to memorise.

plans.reason: Long-diagonal bishops and flank control of the centre.
